body: The first evening in the flat, a woman of twenty-six puts the radio on before she has unpacked anything, because the rooms are empty enough to have an echo in them and the echo is worse than she expected. She is not listening to it. She carries boxes past it, finds the kettle, discovers there is no bin, sits on the floor eating chips out of the paper at half past nine with her coat still on. At some point she notices it is dark outside. She does not turn the radio off before she goes to bed, and in the morning it is still going, and she leaves it, and by the end of the week she has stopped noticing that she never turns it off.
She did not choose a single thing she heard in that flat all week. She chose one thing, once, on the first evening, and then went about her life, and the rest happened without her.
The strongest argument for a radio band over a playlist is not variety. It is that you do not have to decide anything.

The word to take literally here is on. It is the smallest word in the title and it is carrying the whole thing. Something that is on is precisely something nobody is attending to — the moment you attend to it, it is not on any more, it is being listened to, which is a different and much rarer activity. Almost nothing that has formed you arrived while you were attending. It arrived while you were doing the washing-up, or arguing about homework, or driving somewhere you did not want to go. Attention is the narrow gate. Ambience is the wide one, and hardly anybody thinks about what they are letting through it.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air, hosted by the 12 voices of the Inspire Family. Every one of them runs day and night, whether or not anybody has tuned to it.

Programming for a room where nobody is listening closely is a harder discipline than it sounds, and it costs something real. You cannot rely on a hook in the first eight seconds, because there is no first eight seconds — the listener arrives halfway through, or does not arrive at all and simply lets it go past. Every hour has to be safe to have on in a room that might contain a child, or somebody grieving, or somebody who came in to make a sandwich. Nothing can be included because it will get a reaction. That rules out a great deal of perfectly good music, and it is ruled out deliberately.

It is worth saying how strange it has become to let a house have a background at all. The ordinary arrangement now is that every room supplies its own — a phone in one, a television in another, a speaker taking requests in the kitchen — and each of them is chosen, individually, in the moment, by whoever got there first. A household like that has no ambience. It has several private ones running in parallel, each optimised for the person holding the device, and nothing in the building is shared except the walls.

The band is arranged so that a household can pick once and be done with it. The worship and praise formats sit together, country and gospel near one another, the hymn and heritage repertoire in its own stretch, and the children’s frequencies grouped so a parent can land on one without reading anything. You are meant to learn roughly where things are and then stop thinking about it, which is how everybody used a radio, and which no search box has ever permitted.
None of which is an argument against choosing music. It is an argument about what choosing costs, and when.

Be fair to the playlist first. It is precise, it is yours, and it will hand you the exact song you were thinking of before you have finished typing it. But every session opens with an act of curation, and curation takes a kind of energy that is not always available at six in the evening with the dinner on. Worse, a list can only ever return what you already knew to ask for. Left running for a year it will make the house sound more and more like the inside of one person’s head, and the one thing that head badly needs is something arriving in it that did not come from there.
A playlist is a decision you keep having to make. A station is a decision you make once.

In a terraced house on a Tuesday, a woman in her forties is not asking her son any more questions. He is sixteen, he answers in one syllable, and she has worked out that every question she asks makes the next silence heavier. So she stops filling it with questions and starts leaving a station on in the hall instead, quietly, where it can be heard from both the kitchen and the top of the stairs. This goes on for about five weeks. Then on a Tuesday morning, standing at the toaster in his school uniform with his bag already on, he says, turn that up a bit. That is all he says to her before he leaves. She turns it up.
Nothing in that had to be discussed, and nothing had to be agreed. The songs that formed you were mostly not the ones you selected. They were the ones that happened to be on.

There is a real cost to this, and it is not the one people usually name. It is not that a station will play you something you would have skipped, though it will. It is that a house which is never quiet is its own kind of problem. Sound can be used to avoid a room, or a person, or an hour that ought to be sat through without a soundtrack, and a radio left on permanently is one of the easier ways to do that without ever admitting to it.

So the honest version is that leaving it on is not the same as never turning it off. Turn it off when the quiet is the thing that is needed; the point was never noise. But be clear about what the realistic alternative to this station is in most houses, because it is almost never silence. It is the television talking to nobody, or the news on a loop, or three devices in three rooms. Choosing what is ambient is not adding something to a quiet house. It is replacing something that got in without being chosen, and that was designed by people with entirely different aims.

That is the whole recommendation, and it really is that boring. Pick a frequency, leave it on, and let the house have something true in it that nobody has to keep deciding about. Formation is largely a matter of what is ambient, which is exactly why what is ambient is worth choosing once, carefully, and then leaving alone. It is the one thing a library cannot do for you, because a library will not play until it is asked, and the whole value here is in the hours when nobody is asking.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it, whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. Any of them will run all day without being asked anything.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 303.10 — Yes and Amen. It carries the declaration albums, one record for each of the Inspire Family, and what they sing is not a request or a mood but a set of sentences about what is already true. That makes it the right first choice for exactly the argument above. If what is ambient is what forms people, then the most valuable thing to have going quietly in a hallway is not a feeling — it is a settled sentence, arriving again on an ordinary Tuesday while somebody is hunting for their keys and not paying attention. Put it on in the room the house passes through most, and then get on with your day.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a plan. Do not evaluate it and do not sample it — put HM 303.10 on this evening in the room everybody walks through, and then forget about it for a fortnight. Let it play while the dinner burns and the homework gets argued over and nobody in the building is listening to a word of it. At the end of the fortnight somebody in your house will hum something you never played them on purpose, and you will know exactly what this article was about.
